keyVerseText: And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew word אָדָם (ʼâdâm) derives from the root אָדַם (ʼâdam), which means to be red or ruddy. This root sense conveys the idea of redness or a flushed appearance, possibly reflecting the natural color of human skin or the earth from which man was formed. This etymology enriches the common English gloss of 'man' or 'mankind' by emphasizing a physical, earthy origin and a vivid, living presence rather than a mere abstract concept of humanity.
usageInScripture: The word אָדָם appears 553 times in the Old Testament and is most frequently translated as 'man' or 'mankind,' highlighting both the individual human being and the collective human race. Its usage ranges from referring to a single person to humanity as a whole, as seen in the top translations like 'of man' (145 occurrences) and 'of men' (53 occurrences). This broad range underscores the word's flexibility in describing both the particular and the universal aspects of human identity.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding אָדָם as both a physical and relational term deepens our grasp of humanity's role in God's creation. The root meaning of redness or ruddy color connects humanity to the earth, reminding us that we are created beings, formed by God's hand from the dust. Yet, the term also encompasses the dignity of mankind made in God's image, called to steward creation. This dual reality calls believers to humility and responsibility, recognizing our dependence on God and our unique role within His creation plan, ultimately fulfilled in Christ as the true image of God.
keyVerseReflection: Genesis 1:26 declares, 'Let us make man in our image, after our likeness,' highlighting the special status of אָדָם as created in God's image. The use of this word in the verse emphasizes not only the physical humanity but also the spiritual and moral likeness to God that distinguishes mankind. It reminds us that every human being bears the imprint of divine intention and purpose, entrusted with dominion over creation as God's representative on earth.
